methodology.title: How the UV index works
methodology.p1: The UV Index was developed by WHO, the World Meteorological Organization, UNEP, and ICNIRP as a standardized international scale, designed to communicate the intensity of UV radiation at ground level without requiring technical knowledge — before its adoption, every country used different, incomparable scales.
methodology.p2: Actual intensity depends on several factors together: the sun's height in the sky (highest at solar noon and in summer), latitude (stronger near the equator), altitude (increases roughly 10% per 1000 meters, since there's less filtering atmosphere), the thickness of the ozone layer, and cloud cover — this last one is deceptive: even under overcast skies, most UV still gets through, and a common mistake is assuming cloudy weather makes protection unnecessary.
methodology.p3: The number shown in this app is calculated in real time by combining these factors with weather models — that's why it changes hour by hour, peaking near solar noon and dropping close to zero at dawn and dusk, as you can see in the chart above.
methodology.shareText: Cloudy skies don't block most UV — here's how the UV index actually works:

spf.title: How SPF actually works
spf.p1: SPF (Sun Protection Factor) measures how much longer protected skin takes to burn compared to unprotected skin, under lab conditions using a thick, generously applied layer (2 mg per cm²) — in practice, almost no one applies that much, so real-world protection is usually lower than the labeled number.
spf.p2: The relationship between SPF and protection isn't linear: SPF30 blocks about 97% of UVB rays, SPF50 about 98% — a small numerical gap that misleads many people into assuming SPF50 offers roughly double the protection of SPF30. It doesn't. What actually makes the difference is reapplying often and using enough of it, not chasing an ever-higher number.
spf.p3: SPF only measures protection against UVB rays, the ones that cause visible sunburn. A "broad spectrum" label means the product also protects against UVA rays, which penetrate deeper and contribute to skin aging and cancer risk even without causing a visible burn — checking for "broad spectrum" matters as much as the SPF number itself.
spf.shareText: SPF30 blocks ~97% of UVB, SPF50 ~98% — the real difference is reapplying, not chasing a bigger number.

physics.title: The physics behind the number
physics.p1: UV intensity increases by roughly {percent}% for every 1,000 meters of altitude — there's simply less atmosphere above you to filter it. A ski resort at 2,000m can see meaningfully higher UV than the valley below it, on the same clear day.
physics.p2: The sun isn't the only source, either — surfaces bounce a real share of it back up at you. Fresh snow reflects most of it; sand and sea foam matter too, just less dramatically. It's why reflected sunburn (and snow-blindness) are real risks even in the shade.

ozone.title: The ozone layer is healing — here's the actual chart
ozone.p1: Solar UV reaching the ground depends heavily on how much ozone sits between you and space. Industrial chemicals (CFCs) tore a seasonal hole in it over Antarctica starting in the 1980s — by the mid-2000s it had grown to nearly 30 million km², roughly the size of Africa.
ozone.p2: The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased those chemicals out worldwide, and it's working: the hole has been shrinking since around 2000, and current science projects it back to 1980 levels by {year} over Antarctica.

iarc.title: Why UV is officially a Group 1 carcinogen
iarc.intro: Group 1 is the International Agency for Research on Cancer's highest-certainty category — reserved for causes with the strongest human evidence, alongside tobacco and asbestos.

solarUv.text: IARC's Working Group formally classified solar and UV radiation as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1), based on the accumulated epidemiological evidence linking UV exposure to skin cancer.

tanningDevices.text: A separate IARC review extended the same Group 1 classification specifically to UV-emitting tanning devices, after evidence showed melanoma risk rises sharply when tanning-bed use starts before age 30.

privacy.title: Privacy & disclaimer
privacy.metaDescription: What UV Index's numbers do and don't mean, and exactly what happens to your data when you use the app.
privacy.intro: The short version: no accounts, no data for sale, and almost everything about you stays on your own device. Here's the full picture — what this app's guidance does and doesn't mean, and exactly what happens to your data.

notMedicalAdvice.title: Not medical advice
notMedicalAdvice.body: UV Index gives general, population-level sun-safety guidance drawn from public health sources (WHO, the American Academy of Dermatology) and forecast data. It is not medical advice and isn't a substitute for a doctor or dermatologist. Burn-time estimates, reapplication timers, and skin-type guidance are approximations built from published dermatological research, not a personalized risk assessment. If you have a history of skin cancer, take photosensitizing medication, or have a skin condition, follow your clinician's guidance over this app's.

dataAccuracy.title: Data accuracy
dataAccuracy.body: The UV index shown is a forecast from MET Norway's public weather model, not a direct sensor reading at your exact location. Like any forecast, it can be wrong — cloud cover shifts faster than models update, and local conditions (haze, altitude, nearby reflective surfaces) aren't always captured. Treat it as a strong guide, not a guarantee, and trust your own judgement — or an official local warning — over the app if conditions look different.

noLiability.title: No liability
noLiability.body: This is an independent, open-source project, provided as-is and without warranty of any kind. To the fullest extent permitted by law, its author is not liable for sunburn, other harm, or any damages arising from reliance on the information it provides. Use your own judgement outdoors.

controller.title: Who's behind this
controller.body: UV Index is an independent project built and run by Raffaele Pizzari — no company, no data broker, no third party involved beyond the handful of services listed below, each doing exactly one job. For anything privacy-related — questions, requests, or just something that looks off — email:

dataWeCollect.title: What we collect, and why
dataWeCollect.intro: This is the actual GDPR detail: what data moves, where, on what legal basis, and for how long.

location.title: Location (GPS or a searched place)
location.body: When you allow location access or search for a place, your coordinates are sent to our server just long enough to ask MET Norway (and, for search, Open-Meteo or BigDataCloud) for a UV reading — then discarded. We don't write it to a database or attach it to any identity. It's kept only on your own device, so the app can show your last reading if you reopen it offline.
location.legalBasis: Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR — necessary to do the specific thing you asked for.
location.retention: Retention: none — it exists only for the duration of the request.

ip.title: IP address
ip.body: Our API routes briefly hold your IP address in memory to rate-limit requests, so the free tiers of the upstream weather APIs can't be exhausted by one visitor. It lives in server memory only, in a counter that resets every few minutes, and is never written to disk or a database.
ip.legalBasis: Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) — legitimate interest in keeping the service available and within its providers' usage limits.

profile.title: Profile info you enter (name, skin type, infant toggle)
profile.body: Stored entirely in your browser's local storage. It never leaves your device — there's no server-side database for it, so we couldn't see it, export it, or lose it in a breach even if we wanted to. Clearing your browser data deletes it for good.
profile.legalBasis: Legal basis: not applicable — we don't process this data at all.

analytics.title: Anonymous usage analytics
analytics.body: We use Umami, a self-hosted, cookie-free analytics tool, to see aggregate numbers — how many people use the app, which pages get read. Umami sets no cookies and no persistent identifiers, and doesn't store your IP address or anything else that identifies you individually; any country-level stat it derives from IP is computed on the fly, and the address itself is discarded.
analytics.legalBasis: Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) — legitimate interest in basic, non-identifying usage statistics, using a tool chosen specifically because it doesn't need to track anyone.
analytics.retention: Retention: aggregate counts only, kept for as long as they're useful; nothing in them identifies you.

thirdParties.title: Who else sees a request
thirdParties.intro: Getting you a UV reading means forwarding your coordinates to whichever of these does that specific job — nobody else.
thirdParties.met: MET Norway — the UV forecast itself.
thirdParties.openMeteo: Open-Meteo — turning a typed place name into coordinates.
thirdParties.bigDataCloud: BigDataCloud — turning GPS coordinates into a place name.
thirdParties.umami: Umami, self-hosted on our own infrastructure — anonymous usage counts.
thirdParties.note: None of these receive anything that identifies you personally, and we don't share data with advertisers, data brokers, or anyone else. Some may process requests on infrastructure outside the EU/EEA; where that's the case, it's on them to secure it under their own compliance obligations (e.g. standard contractual clauses).

cookiesStorage.title: Cookies and local storage
cookiesStorage.body: This app sets no cookies. Everything it remembers about you — profiles, skin type, notification preferences, saved places, your last known reading — lives in your browser's local storage, on your device only, and is never transmitted to our servers. Clear it any time from your browser's site settings; the app just starts fresh next time.

yourRights.title: Your rights
yourRights.intro: Because so little personal data is processed server-side, most of these are already satisfied by design — but formally, under the GDPR, you have the right to:
yourRights.access: Access — know what data concerning you we process (as above, that's minimal and mostly nothing).
yourRights.rectification: Rectification — correct anything inaccurate. For your locally-stored profile, that's a Settings screen away.
yourRights.erasure: Erasure — ask us to delete data we hold. There's essentially nothing server-side to delete; for local data, clearing your browser storage does it instantly.
yourRights.restriction: Restriction & objection — object to or restrict processing based on legitimate interest (the IP rate-limiting and analytics above).
yourRights.portability: Portability — receive data you provided in a portable format, where applicable.
yourRights.complaint: Complaint — lodge one with your local data protection authority; in Italy, that's the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (garanteprivacy.it).
yourRights.outro: To exercise any of these, email:

children.title: Children
children.body: The app's "infant" toggle exists purely to switch its sun-safety guidance — AAP/AAD recommendations are that infants under 6 months avoid direct sun entirely rather than rely on a burn-time budget. It isn't a data-collection feature, and like the rest of profile data, it's stored on-device only. We don't knowingly collect personal data from children beyond what any visitor's device already handles locally.

changes.title: Changes to this page
